title: LangGraph essentials
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic quizzes that follow the backend interview roadmap: language core, concurrency, DSA habits, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, and LLM/agent engineering.
description: StateGraph state and reducers, routing, checkpointers and threads, human-in-the-loop, streaming modes, limits, multi-agent patterns and designing a copilot graph.
source: Interview roadmap study plan (Java/Spring Boot and Python/FastAPI)

questions.prompt: In a LangGraph StateGraph, two parallel nodes in the same step both update a state key that has no reducer. What happens?

options.text: The graph raises an error, as it cannot merge concurrent updates without a reducer.
options.why: Right: define a reducer, such as list concatenation, for keys written concurrently.

options.text: The last node to finish silently wins, so the earlier update is overwritten without notice.
options.why: LangGraph refuses rather than guessing a winner for concurrent writes.

options.text: The values are combined into a list automatically so that nothing is lost.
options.why: Merging happens only where you declare a reducer for the key.

options.text: The first node to finish wins and the later write is dropped by the checkpointer.
options.why: There is no first-wins rule, and the checkpointer does not arbitrate writes.

questions.explanation: A reducer defines how an update combines with the existing value (for example appending to a message list). Keys written by one node at a time can stay plain overwrite.

questions.prompt: In the supervisor multi-agent pattern, what is the supervisor's job?

options.text: Decide which worker agent or node runs next, and when to finish, based on the shared state.
options.why: Right: it routes work; workers do the specialised tasks and report back.

options.text: Run every worker's tools itself so that the workers only supply prompts to it.
options.why: Workers own their tools; the supervisor coordinates.

options.text: Replace the checkpointer by storing the conversation history inside its own prompt.
options.why: Persistence is a separate concern handled by the checkpointer.

options.text: Merge all worker outputs into one answer without ever choosing among workers.
options.why: Routing is the defining responsibility; summarising is optional.

questions.explanation: Subgraphs let each worker be its own graph with private state. Interview point: supervisors add an extra model call per hop, so measure latency and cost.

questions.prompt: A copilot must send some questions to a tool-using retrieval path and others to a text-to-SQL path. What is the sound graph design?

options.text: A conditional edge whose router reads state, such as intent, and returns the next node.
options.why: Right: routing is exactly what conditional edges are for.

options.text: Normal edges to both paths so every question runs both, keeping whichever answer returns first.
options.why: That wastes cost and can return the wrong path's answer.

options.text: One giant node that contains both paths with if statements, hiding the branch from the graph.
options.why: You lose per-node tracing, retries and checkpoints.

options.text: A random edge choice with a retry whenever the answer looks poor to the user.
options.why: Random routing is unreliable and slow to correct.

questions.explanation: Keep routers cheap and testable: a small classifier or rules with a fallback branch for unclear intent, and eval the router separately.

questions.prompt: What do you get by compiling a graph with a checkpointer and invoking it with a thread_id?

options.text: State is saved per thread after each step, so the same thread_id continues the run.
options.why: Right: this gives conversation memory, resumption and time-travel debugging.

options.text: Nodes run in parallel across threads, which speeds up each single request noticeably.
options.why: thread_id identifies saved state; it does not parallelise nodes.

options.text: All users share one long-term memory automatically, because threads are global.
options.why: Threads are isolated; cross-thread memory needs a separate store.

options.text: LLM responses are cached by thread so repeated prompts skip the model call.
options.why: Checkpoints store graph state, not a response cache.

questions.explanation: Use a durable checkpointer (for example backed by Postgres) in production, since in-memory checkpoints vanish on restart.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply. A copilot must pause for human approval before a risky tool call and later continue. What does this rely on?

options.text: A checkpointer, so the paused state is saved and survives while waiting.
options.why: Right: without persistence there is nothing to resume.

options.text: A thread_id, which identifies which paused run the decision belongs to.
options.why: Right: the resume call targets the same thread.

options.text: A resume call that supplies the human's decision, so the graph continues from the interrupt.
options.why: Right: the interrupt returns the value you pass on resume.

options.text: A worker thread blocked on console input for the whole approval period.
options.why: Blocking holds resources and is lost on restart; use persisted state.

options.text: Turning checkpointing off so that stale state cannot be reused by the approval step.
options.why: Disabling checkpoints removes the ability to pause and resume.

questions.explanation: Interrupt and resume turns approval into an asynchronous workflow, which can span hours. Re-run safe checks on resume because the world may have changed.

questions.prompt: In LangGraph, the updates stream mode emits only what each node changed, while values emits the full state after every step.

options.text: True
options.why: Right: updates are per-node deltas; values are full snapshots; messages streams LLM tokens.

options.text: False
options.why: The modes differ in granularity as stated.

questions.explanation: Pick by use case: messages for typing effects, updates for progress UI, values for debugging or full-state consumers.

questions.prompt: The recursion limit in LangGraph caps how many seconds a single node may run before it is cancelled.

options.text: True
options.why: It is a time cap.

options.text: False
options.why: Right: it limits the number of steps in a run and raises an error when exceeded, guarding against loops.

questions.explanation: Time limits are per-node timeouts you add yourself, and retry policies are configured per node. The recursion limit stops runaway agent loops; also bound tool-retry counts in state.

questions.prompt: In an 11-node text-to-SQL copilot graph, where should SQL safety validation live?

options.text: A deterministic node between generation and execution, looping back with the error a few times.
options.why: Right: code checks the query before it can touch the database.

options.text: Inside the generator's system prompt, asking the model to be careful about dangerous queries.
options.why: A prompt is a request, not an enforced control.

options.text: After execution, by checking the returned rows for anything that looks wrong or sensitive.
options.why: The query has already run, so any damage or leak has happened.

options.text: In the final answer formatter, which rewrites unsafe wording before the user sees it.
options.why: Formatting text does not stop an unsafe query from executing.

questions.explanation: A typical graph has nodes like intake, intent router, retrieval, schema fetch, SQL generation, SQL validation, execution, result check, answer synthesis, approval and audit. Give each node one responsibility, per-node retry and timeout policies, and an explicit failure edge.
